lesson.title: Beyond Straight Lines: Meet the Quadratic Function
lesson.summary: A quadratic function is a polynomial function whose highest-degree term is x squared, and that single change from degree 1 to degree 2 is what allows its graph to curve instead of staying straight.
lesson.body:
Recall two ideas you already have. A function is a rule that assigns exactly one output to each input. A polynomial is an expression built from terms with whole-number exponents on the variable, added or subtracted together. A quadratic function combines both ideas in a specific way: it is a polynomial function whose highest exponent, or degree, is exactly 2. In general form, a quadratic function looks like f(x) = ax^2 + bx + c, where a, b, and c are real numbers and a cannot equal 0.

That last restriction matters more than it might seem. If a were 0, the x^2 term would vanish entirely and you would be left with f(x) = bx + c, which is just a linear function. So a ≠ 0 is what actually makes the function quadratic rather than linear, it guarantees the x^2 term survives.

Why does one extra exponent matter so much? In a linear function, the output changes by the same fixed amount, the slope, every time the input increases by 1. In a quadratic function, that is no longer true: the rate of change itself keeps changing as x changes. That single fact is why quadratics can model things a straight line never could, the height of a thrown ball that rises then falls, the area enclosed by a fence of fixed length as you vary its shape, or profit that increases with more sales up to a point and then decreases. All of those situations have a turning point, and only a curved graph can capture that.

Evaluating a quadratic function works exactly like evaluating any other function: substitute the input for x and simplify using order of operations. Take f(x) = 2x^2 - 3x + 1. To find f(3), substitute 3 for every x: f(3) = 2(3)^2 - 3(3) + 1 = 2(9) - 9 + 1 = 18 - 9 + 1 = 10. To find f(-2), substitute -2, being careful with the sign since it gets squared: f(-2) = 2(-2)^2 - 3(-2) + 1 = 2(4) + 6 + 1 = 8 + 6 + 1 = 15. Notice that squaring the input makes negative inputs produce positive contributions from the x^2 term, which is part of why quadratic graphs end up symmetric, a property you will explore closely in the next few sections.
